item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Votes don't help the author, so I've vowed to always leave a comment with mine, at the very least whenever I rate an article negatively. If you feel the same, help out by leaving critique with more of your votes. Comment follows:

There's nothing particularly unique about the concept - both D-class production and salesman personality as a -J have been done before (I think). There's nothing particularly unique about the execution. Actually, there's nothing here that flashes in your face. It's a unified, simmering piece that doesn't overstep its bounds. It's not flashy, but it works.

I like the dialogue. It's understated and feels realistic, as far as the context permits. There's few jokes, as such, just naturally amusing dialogue. Though where there are jokes - like "Why does everything have to be a story, now?!" - it doesn't work too well. That section would be better off without that line and its leadup. I also don't like the deviations from clinical tone in the description and containment procedures, which detract from that understated feeling for me.

Overall, I found this more consistently mildly amusing than hilarious. However, my criteria for voting on -Js is whether or not I laughed, and "They ate the other one" had me in brief hysterics, so that's that.

item.content:encoded:
I can get down with a critique of the usage of D-Class throughout the site's history, but the actual execution of this piece isn't particularly convincing me. The non-clinical, comedically slanted documentation feels extremely bog-standard and doesn't differentiate itself that well from the many other joke SCPs with that specific quirk, and the dialogue just failed to surprise me all that much, and often felt way too on-the-nose in its satire for my liking (Polk's long paragraph at the end exemplifies this for me).

Overall, there just isn't anything all that new or exceptional about how it was executed, and as such this didn't get much of a reaction out of me.

-1.
